sections.body:
Loneliness is the feeling that the connection you want is not there. It behaves like a feeling: it can arrive in a full room and disappear in an empty one, it can be stronger on a Sunday than on a Thursday, and nobody else can see it from the outside. It is not a count of the people around you, and it is not a measurement of anything you can point at afterwards.

The **fact** of being alone is a different thing. Alone means that nobody is there; lonely means that the connection you want is not there. A person can be alone and not lonely. A person can sit in a room full of colleagues and be lonely. Only the fact is visible from outside: a colleague can see that you went home alone, and cannot see that the evening was empty. This is why the two are so easily confused. When somebody says 'I am lonely', they are reporting a feeling; when somebody else says 'you must be lonely', they are guessing at a fact.

Three neighbouring words have their own meanings. **Isolation** is the condition of being separated from other people: it can be physical, when nobody is in the room; social, when you know nobody here; or emotional, when the people are there and you are not part of it. **Alienation** is the state of being estranged, from the people around you, from a group you belong to, or from your own life while you are living it; it can be a position you are in and a feeling about that position at the same time. **Solitude** is being alone as a condition, chosen or at least not distressing. Solitude is the neutral word. Loneliness is the word that names a distress solitude does not have to carry.

How much of loneliness comes from the situation and how much from the person is not settled, and the two accounts do not cancel each other. One account puts most of it in the condition of your life: the number of people who know you, the work, the hours, the money, the health. Another puts it in the expectation: two people in the same room can feel completely different, and what each of them notices decides more than what is on the table. Researchers also disagree about how far a change of surroundings can move the feeling, and about how much of the change has to come from inside. Nothing in this article depends on winning that argument. What is not in dispute is that the feeling is real, and that the four words above point at four different things.
examples: Loneliness is the feeling that the connection you want is not there; being alone is the fact that nobody is there.
I am not alone, I am lonely, and those are two different things.
They were in a full room, and she was lonely anyway.
sections.heading: Loneliness is a feeling, being alone is a fact

terms.example: He was in a full room and lonely anyway.
terms.gloss: The feeling that the connection you want is not there.

terms.example: Work took him to a site where isolation was part of the job.
terms.gloss: The condition of being separated from other people, in body, in company or in feeling.

terms.example: He worked in the same team for years and felt alienated from it.
terms.gloss: The state of being estranged from the people around you, from a group, or from your own life.

terms.example: She reads for an hour every evening, and she calls it solitude.
terms.gloss: Being alone as a condition, chosen or at least not distressing.

sections.body:
Selectivity is the practice of choosing fewer people and refusing more of them, so that the people who are chosen get more of you. It is not the same as being hard to please. Selectivity is a policy: it has a standard, a method and a cost, and the person applying it usually knows all three.

Four things raise the bar. The first is a **standard**: a clear picture of what you want, built partly from what you have already seen and partly from what you have been told a good match looks like. The second is a past disappointment, which stays in the memory longer than it deserves to, because a bad match costs weeks of a life and is not refunded. The third is fatigue: a new person costs attention, and after a long day the attention is already spent, so the answer comes out before the person has been looked at. The fourth is the price of a bad match, and it is the engine behind the other three. When the downside is high, the expected value of saying yes falls, and a stricter test looks like prudence.

This is the trade-off, and it is not free. A high bar raises the quality of a match and lowers the number of candidates. The more dimensions you require, the fewer people survive the test. When the required match has to be exact on every dimension, the ideal is **hyperfidelity**: the belief that one person will match a complete specification without any deviation, and that a deviation makes it a failure. A specification with many dimensions and no tolerance rejects nearly every candidate, which is the quiet way a search ends before it has really started.

From the inside, the two sides of the trade-off look exactly the same, because the people who would have come through a lower door never arrive. The silence after a refusal feels like proof that the bar was right. The cost of a closed door is invisible by construction, and that is the mechanism that keeps a closed door closed. Whether selectivity is good judgement or avoidance is not settled, and this article will not settle it. One account says a clear standard is simply accurate self-knowledge: a person knows what they need and refuses to spend another year on a near miss. Another says that a bar which nobody clears is a way of arranging never to be disappointed again, and that the refusal does the work that courage would do. The two accounts are not exclusive, and the difference between them is not visible from the inside. What is visible is whether the standard can be stated in one sentence, and whether it moves every time somebody comes close. A standard that can be said and a standard that hides are different objects, and only one of them can be examined.
examples: A high bar buys a better match and costs you the candidates who would have come through it.
I can state my standard in one sentence, and I would rather be judged by it.
Nobody matches a complete specification exactly, so a search like that never ends well.
sections.heading: Why the bar goes up, and what a closed door costs

terms.example: Her selectivity is not rudeness; it is a policy she applies to everybody.
terms.gloss: The practice of choosing fewer people and refusing more, so that the chosen ones get more of you.

terms.example: He could not say what his standard was, and that was the problem.
terms.gloss: The test a person applies when choosing, expressed in terms of what that person wants.

terms.example: Hyperfidelity is why the search stops before it has really begun.
terms.gloss: The belief that a partner must match a complete specification exactly, with no deviation allowed.

sections.body:
Two words describe what you have with other people. **Connection** is a link that carries something in both directions: attention, information, care, obligation. A link that carries nothing in one direction is not a connection, and it is worth noticing which direction is empty. **Mutuality** is the state in which both sides give and both receive, and the test of it is simple: each person can say what the other gives them. If only one of them can answer that question, the link is not mutual, whatever the two of them call it.

Two words describe what you are aiming at. **Commitment** is a decision to keep something going at a cost to yourself, and the word describes a sequence rather than a moment: it is made again every time you turn up, every time you choose the difficult conversation over the easy exit, every time you make room in the week. **Commitment readiness** is the state of being able to make that decision now: having the time, the wish, and a picture of what it will cost. Readiness is not the same as wanting. A person can want a relationship very much and be not ready, and the two are often confused, including by the person who has them.

Two words describe your posture and your history. **Openness** is the willingness to be known by somebody new, and it is wider than selectivity: a selective person is often open with the people who have been chosen, and an open person can still refuse many people. **Aversion** is a strong dislike that turns a possible approach into an immediate withdrawal. It is often learned rather than chosen, it can be about one person and it can be about a whole category of people, and it does not always know what it is protecting.

One word names the mechanism underneath. An **approach-avoidance conflict** is the state in which the same goal pulls you towards it and away from it at the same time: the wish for a partner makes you reach out, and the wish not to be disappointed makes you withdraw. Nothing has gone wrong in this situation. Both halves are answering the same question honestly, and they are answering it with opposite answers.
examples: A connection exists only if both sides put something into it.
Mutuality is the test: each of us can say what the other gives.
Commitment is a sequence of small decisions, not one switch.
I am open to a relationship, and I am not ready to commit to one yet.
sections.heading: The words of choosing, connecting and committing

terms.example: They have a connection, and every few weeks it carries something in both directions.
terms.gloss: A link that carries something in both directions: attention, information, care or obligation.

terms.example: There is no mutuality here: one of them does all the giving.
terms.gloss: The state in which both sides give and both receive, checked by asking each side what the other gives.

terms.example: Commitment is not one decision; it is the tenth one as well as the first.
terms.gloss: A decision to keep something going at a cost to yourself, made again and again rather than once.

terms.example: He has the wish and not the readiness, and he can tell the two apart.
terms.gloss: The state of being able to make the decision of commitment now, with the time, the wish and a picture of the cost.

terms.example: Openness is not saying yes to everybody; it is letting one more person in.
terms.gloss: The willingness to be known by somebody new, which is wider than being selective or not.

terms.example: Her aversion to that kind of meeting turned into a refusal before she had read the message.
terms.gloss: A strong dislike that turns a possible approach into an immediate withdrawal.

terms.example: The approach-avoidance conflict is inside him, not in the other person.
terms.gloss: The state in which the same goal pulls you towards it and away from it at the same time.

sections.body:
The common picture of commitment is a switch: you decide once, and afterwards you live inside the decision. The reality is duller and more useful. Commitment is made again and again, in small decisions that each have the same shape: you give something up now for something later. You turn up on the day you did not want to. You choose the awkward conversation over the easy exit. You keep the promise that costs you an evening. Nobody makes all of these at once, and nobody has to be brave at the beginning of a relationship in order to make them later.

Two halves of the person are active in each of these decisions. The **approach half** reaches out: it makes contact, it stays in the room, it accepts the risk of being known. What it protects is the possibility of a good outcome, and it cannot protect that on its own, because a good outcome needs the other side to move as well. The **avoidance half** withdraws: it keeps the options open, it does not spend the last evening, it protects itself from the disappointment of a bad match. What it protects is real too: the time, the energy, and the part of a life that a bad match would take.

Because both halves are answering the same question at the same time, they pull in opposite directions. This is an approach-avoidance conflict, and it explains a pattern that puzzles people: the contact comes in bursts. A message is sent, an invitation is made, a plan is proposed; then the avoidance half takes over, the replies get shorter, and the contact dies without a moment that anyone could point at. The bursts are not a sign of what the person really wants. They are the visible trace of two answers arriving together.

How much of that balance belongs to the person and how much to the situation is not settled. Some accounts put it in the history: what an earlier relationship taught, what a family looked like, what was lost. Other accounts put it in the situation itself: how many people are available, what the work allows, how long it takes to meet anybody in a new city. Both accounts describe something real, and they are not exclusive. The practical consequence is the same either way. The way through is not to remove the avoidance half: it has a reason, and it is protecting something the person actually values. The way through is to make the next decision small enough to be made while both halves are still pulling.
examples: Commitment is not one decision; it is the tenth one as well as the first.
The avoidance half protected his weekends, and it also emptied them.
The next decision is small enough to make today, even with both halves pulling.
sections.heading: Commitment is made one decision at a time

sections.body:
The two columns in the table are not opposites, and they are not stages. A person can be highly selective and deeply committed at the same time, to a small number of people. A person can be open and uncommitted. The columns are better read as two answers to the same question: what am I protecting? Selectivity protects your time and your attention. Commitment protects a relationship, and it costs you the freedom to leave.

Read one row as a signal and not as a proof. Almost every signal below can be produced by either column: short replies can come from a busy week or from a decision to stop; a fixed plan can come from a careful standard or from an attachment that has already decided. A signal becomes useful when three of them point the same way, and when they have pointed that way for a while rather than for a day.

The last row is the practical one. What usually helps in the selectivity column is a change in the terms of the meeting: say the standard out loud, make the first meeting cheap, and let repeated contact do the rest. What usually helps in the commitment column is a change in the size of the next decision: make it small enough to make, and keep the cost of staying visible to the other person.
examples: Three signals that point the same way are worth more than one signal that points hard.
Selectivity protects your time; commitment protects the relationship.
I am saying my standard out loud, so you can check it.
sections.heading: Selectivity and commitment, side by side

rows: Every possible match is checked against a list before anything happens.
The decision is made again, small, each time it is needed.
Fewer candidates and less contact, and a bar that may never be met.
Time, money, and the freedom to leave at any point.
The weeks and the energy that a bad match would cost.
The relationship, by keeping the ordinary effort in it.
Distance: short replies, few plans, no second meeting.
Attention that does not drift, and time that is kept.
Say the standard in one sentence, and make the first meeting cheap.
Make the next decision small, and keep the cost of staying visible.

sections.body:
None of this is a treatment, and none of it is supposed to change anybody's life. It is maintenance: five moves that change the cost of the ordinary parts of a social life. They work whether the reader is lonely, selective, committed, or simply alone on a Thursday evening.

The first three steps work on the supply side: the number of people who are there, and how easy it is to reach them. The fourth step works on the wish, by separating two desires that are usually carried by one word. The fifth step works on the decision, by making the thing you are willing to give concrete enough to act on.

The order is not important, and none of the steps needs a tool. What matters is that the first three are cheap and repeatable, because a habit that needs a special occasion does not survive a busy month.
examples: I call two people a week, and I do not need a reason to call them.
The first meeting is a coffee between two commitments, and that is the whole idea.
I want a witness, and I want a partner, and they are not the same thing.
This is what I am prepared to give: time, attention, and the difficult conversations.
sections.heading: Five things you can actually do
steps: Keep the connections that already exist. Choose the two or three people you would call if something went wrong, and contact them without a reason attached. A connection is maintained by use, not by intention: the link decays when nothing goes along it, whatever the intention was.

Lower the cost of the first meeting. Make it short, cheap and repeatable: a coffee between two commitments, a walk, a phone call. The cost of a first meeting is exactly what selectivity is usually defending against, so lowering it lowers the need for the defence.

Widen the circle of people who know you. Not more people: more places where you are seen repeatedly, such as a class, a club, a shift, a project or a volunteering group. People who meet once are a stranger; people who meet three times are a different proposition, and the second and third meeting are cheaper for both of you.

Separate the wish for a partner from the wish for a witness. A partner is somebody who shares the ordinary days and the practical work of a life. A witness is somebody who hears about your days and knows what happened. Both wishes are real, and only one of them is answered by a partner. Naming which one you are carrying stops the other from doing all the work.

Decide what you are actually willing to give. Commitment is a sequence of decisions, so the sequence needs something to be made of: time, attention, money, space, honesty about the difficult things, availability on an ordinary Wednesday. A person who has written this down can make the next small decision. A person who has not cannot, however much they want to.

sections.body:
Loneliness is not a character defect. It is a feeling, and it is produced by a life in its current shape: the work, the hours, the money, the health, the people who are there and the people who are not. A person who feels it is not carrying a moral failure, and this article gives no test that ranks one life above another. Nothing here is a diagnosis either.

Being selective is not the same as being closed. Selectivity has a standard, and a standard can be written down and argued with. Closedness has no standard that can be examined, because the answer changes with whoever is standing at the door. One of the two is a practice a person applies and can revise; the other is a way of being unavailable that is rarely available for revision. Which one is happening is something only the person doing it can say.

A long single period is a period, not a verdict. Years without a partner describe a stretch of a life, the same way a long night shift describes a stretch of a life. A stretch has a beginning, a middle and, possibly, an end, and none of that is a score. And none of this article tells the reader which they ought to be. A person may be lonely, selective, committed, or alone and content; all four are positions in the same vocabulary, and the job of the vocabulary is to let a conversation happen without guessing.
examples: Loneliness is a feeling, not a defect.
Being selective is not the same as being closed, and the difference is whether the standard can be said out loud.
A long single period is a period. It is not a score.
sections.heading: Three things this article does not say

sections.body:
Four situations, four sets of sentences. The first is saying you are lonely without apologising for it. The second is answering the well-meaning person who has a candidate in mind. The third is saying what commitment means to you, in words the other person can act on. The fourth is admitting that you are not ready, which is a piece of information and not a refusal.

Say them plainly. The sentence is short, it names the thing, and it does not need a second sentence of apology attached to it. If the other person wants to argue, that is a separate conversation and it can happen on its own.
examples: I have been lonely for a while, and I am not going to pretend otherwise.
I am not alone, I am lonely, and those are two different things.
It has been a quiet few months. I would like that to change.
Thank you for thinking of me. I am not dating at the moment, and I appreciate it.
I met somebody last month and it did not work out, so I am taking it slowly.
I know you mean well. I will tell you if that changes.
For me, commitment is turning up on an ordinary Wednesday, not on a special occasion.
I commit in small steps: a call, a plan, the same time each week.
I am willing to give time and attention, and I am not ready to share a home yet.
I am not ready to be in a relationship, and I would rather say so than pretend.
I like meeting people. I am not ready to commit.
Not yet. Ask me again in the spring.
sections.heading: Sentences you can use

item.summary: Loneliness is a feeling, and being alone is a fact, and the two are easily confused. After reading this you can tell loneliness, isolation, alienation and solitude apart, explain why a standard rises and what a closed door costs, describe commitment as a series of small decisions, and say what you want from a relationship in sentences you can use.
item.title: Loneliness, Selectivity and Commitment
